📉
Trend — Filtered Selection
Most OECD countries have reduced ALOS since 2000 — from ~8.4 to ~6.4 days — reflecting advances in day surgery, care coordination, and discharge planning.
⚠️
Highest ALOS in View
Japan (26d) and Korea (17d) report significantly higher ALOS than peers, driven largely by long psychiatric and rehabilitation stays — not acute care inefficiency alone.
🎯
Efficiency Benchmark in View
Türkiye (4.2d) and Mexico (4.7d) achieve the lowest ALOS, suggesting high-throughput models. However, early discharge risks should also be monitored.

🌍
ALOS Disparity in View
Japan's 26-day ALOS vs Türkiye's 4.2 days is a 6× gap — driven by care model differences, not just clinical need. System design matters enormously.
📊
Beds & ALOS Correlated
Countries with more beds per 1,000 tend to have longer average stays (r≈0.6). More capacity creates incentive to fill beds beyond clinical necessity.
💡
Convergence / Variance
The variance in ALOS across OECD has narrowed since 2000, suggesting global reforms — day surgery, integrated care — are reducing systemic inequality.

🔗
Correlation Insight
Beds and ALOS show a strong positive correlation (r=0.79, R²=0.63) — countries with more hospital beds per capita consistently have longer stays. This suggests capacity itself may shape utilisation behaviour, not just clinical need.
💻
Digital Health Signal
Digital health maturity varies widely across the filtered selection — see the Digital Health Adoption tab for the full category breakdown.
🎯
Prescriptive Insight
Japan and Korea both sit in the "high ALOS + high beds" quadrant — a systemic overcapacity pattern. Netherlands and Mexico sit in "low ALOS + low beds" — lean, high-throughput models worth benchmarking.
